# The Last Ferry on Lake Verrin

Marta had run the ferry across Lake Verrin for thirty-one years, and every year the crossing got shorter.

When she started, it took forty minutes. Her father had taught her to read the water: the dark patches where the wind came down off the ridge, the pale stretches over the sandbars, the place near the middle where the lake went so deep it looked like a hole in the world. She learned to time the engine's cough and the way the hull answered her hand. She learned which passengers wanted to talk and which wanted the water to themselves.

Now the crossing took nine minutes, and the deep place was mud.

Nobody in town said the lake was dying. They said *low*, the way you say a relative is *tired*. It had been a dry decade. The snow on the ridge came late and left early. The docks had been extended twice, then abandoned, and their ends stood in the air like diving boards over an empty pool. Children walked out to the old waterline and picked up things the lake had been keeping: bottles, a bicycle, a single ladies' shoe, and once, wrapped in rotted canvas, a violin that had swelled into a shape like a sleeping fish.

The ferry was called the *Ondine*. She was twenty-two feet of scarred fiberglass and stubbornness, with a bench down each side and a canopy that leaked in exactly three places. Marta knew all three. She kept a coffee can under the worst one, and the sound of rain on it was how she told the time in winter.

On the first Tuesday of October, a man in clean boots was waiting at the east landing with a tripod and a yellow case.

"Are you running?" he asked.

"I'm always running," said Marta. "Nobody's always riding."

He laughed, a little too politely, and climbed aboard. He set the case between his feet as though it might escape. She pushed off, and the *Ondine* slid out over water the color of weak tea.

"I'm with the county," he said. "Hydrology."

"Ah."

"I'm supposed to take some measurements. Depth, mostly. Inflow."

"You'll want the middle," Marta said. "It won't take you long."

He looked at her, then at the shore they were already leaving behind. "I was told this was a forty-minute crossing."

"It was."

They rode in silence for a while. A heron stood on a mudbank and watched them pass with the disapproval of a landlord. The engine muttered. Somewhere under the hull, the lakebed unrolled itself in slow gray folds, and Marta could feel it the way you feel a stair in the dark.

"Can I ask you something?" the man said. His name was Peter; he'd said so and she had already forgotten, then remembered, then decided to keep it. "Why do you keep doing it? There's a road now. It's twelve minutes around the north end. Nobody needs a boat."

Marta considered lying, or joking. But he had the look of someone who'd come a long way to be told something true, even if he didn't know it.

"My father used to say the ferry wasn't for getting across," she said. "It was for the middle. You leave one side, you haven't arrived at the other, and for a little while you belong to neither. People need that more than they know. They sit here and say things they wouldn't say on land. I've heard confessions. I've heard proposals. A woman once told me she was leaving her husband, right there, where you're sitting, and then she rode back with me and *didn't* leave him, and I don't think either choice was wrong. It was just the middle that let her look at it."

Peter said nothing. He looked at the water.

"Now the middle's nine minutes," Marta said. "Next year, maybe six. I keep thinking there's a number where it stops being a middle at all. Where it's just a puddle you step over." She shrugged. "I haven't found the number yet, so I keep going."

He opened the yellow case. Inside was a sounding line with a weight like a fat brass teardrop, a folded chart, a small instrument with a screen. He didn't use any of them. He held the weight in his palm, as if it were a bird's egg.

"The inflow's gone," he said finally. "That's what I'm here to write. The spring that fed it has shifted underground. It's not coming back, not in our lifetimes. They're going to recommend the county stop maintaining the landings."

"I know," said Marta.

"You *know*?"

"I've known for six years. The lake told me. It's not subtle." She eased the throttle, and the *Ondine* drifted into the very center, over where the deep place used to be. The mud below was pocked and shining. "Take your measurement."

He dropped the weight over the side. It fell four feet and stopped with a soft, unimpressive tug.

"Four feet, two inches," Peter said, and wrote it down. His pen paused. "This is the bit I don't know how to put in a report."

"Then leave it out."

"I can't."

"No," Marta agreed. "But you can put it somewhere else."

They sat there, the engine off, the boat turning slowly on its own small axis. A wind came down from the ridge and crossed the water in a dark patch, exactly where her father had said it would. Peter watched it come. It touched the boat and passed, and for a moment the whole lake seemed to breathe in.

"What'll you do?" he asked. "After."

"I thought I'd row," said Marta. "Once the engine's pointless. Then walk it, when it's dry. I'll carry the bench across if I have to. Somebody will want to sit on it."

He smiled at that, really smiled, and she liked him for it.

She started the engine again and turned the *Ondine* toward the west landing, which was close now, close enough that she could see a child on the dock's bare end, waving with her whole arm. Behind them the wake spread thin and brief across the tea-colored water, closing almost as soon as it opened.

"Same fare as always," Marta said. "Two dollars. Four if you make me talk."

Peter paid her four.
